title: Introduction
preview: This chapter presents the security architecture integrated into . The goal of the security layer is not to transform the platform into a full enterprise zero-trust environment, but to ensure that the final deployment already includes meaningful protection mechanisms for identity, browser access, sensitive service exposure, remote operations, and persisted runtime data. The implemented controls are grounded in standar
preview2: d secure-service principles rather than improvised protections .

title: Security Objectives
preview: The security work of the project follows five main objectives: authenticate critical distributed services rather than relying on implicit trust; secure browser-facing administrative or analytical interfaces; protect exposed endpoints through encryption in transit; reduce the operational risk of remote orchestration actions; strengthen the protection of service data persisted on the virtual machines. title: Kerberos-Secured Hadoop Services
preview: Kerberos is the core identity mechanism used to secure the Hadoop side of the platform. In a distributed environment, services such as the NameNode and DataNodes should not trust requests only because they originate from another cluster component. They must validate the identity of the caller explicitly . In the implementation, the Kerberos KDC and administration service are hosted on VM2, which is already the coordi
preview2: nation-heavy node of the data plane. This is consistent with the overall architecture: the node that centralizes namespace and metadata authority also centralizes identity management for the secure Hadoop runtime. title: SPNEGO-Protected HDFS Browser Access
preview: The HDFS browser path is protected through SPNEGO layered on top of the Kerberos-based identity model. This means that access to the secured NameNode and DataNode web interfaces is not treated as a public or weakly protected administrative convenience. It becomes part of the authenticated architecture . From a report perspective, this feature is important because administrative web interfaces are often overlooked in
preview2: student projects even when the back-end services are secured. Here, the platform extends the security posture to the browser-facing HDFS access path. title: TLS-Protected Interfaces
preview: TLS is used to protect the main browser-facing interfaces of the platform. The implemented objective is not to wrap every internal port blindly, but to secure the access paths that matter most for demonstration, administration, and analytical interaction. In this sense, transport protection complements identity protection rather than replacing it . Two main exposure zones are protected: the HDFS browser interfaces th
preview2: rough HTTPS; the Trino analytical access gateway through HTTPS. The local control-plane interfaces are also exposed through a local TLS gateway, which reinforces a consistent secured-access posture for Airflow, Grafana, Prometheus, and Kafka UI. title: Authenticated Trino Access
preview: Trino is not exposed as an open analytical endpoint. Instead, the project implements an authenticated gateway in front of the coordinator-side browser access path. This has two important effects : it reduces uncontrolled direct access to the analytical query service; it demonstrates that user-facing SQL access must also respect basic identity and access boundaries. The gateway is hosted on VM2 together with the Trino
preview2: coordinator, which is consistent with the node's role as the entry point for coordination-heavy services. Through this design, the browser-facing access path is separated from the internal worker topology. Users connect to the protected entry point, while the internal distributed Trino execution still takes place through the coordinator and worker nodes. title: SSH-Based Remote Spark Submission
preview: The orchestration model of the project relies on a remote Spark submission path from the control plane to VM2. This was introduced to avoid unstable local-driver assumptions and to keep the operational launch path aligned with the distributed cluster environment. title: Encrypted Runtime Storage Support
preview: The project also introduces support for encrypted runtime storage through LUKS on the Linux virtual machines. This measure targets rather than only service authentication or traffic encryption . In practice, this control is intended to protect runtime service data stored on VM1, VM2, and VM3. The main idea is that a distributed platform should not protect data movement while leaving persisted service data entirely un
preview2: protected. Even in an academic setup, demonstrating this distinction is valuable because it shows a more complete understanding of security dimensions. The implemented logic therefore complements the other controls: Kerberos protects identity, SPNEGO protects browser negotiation, TLS protects exposed traffic, LUKS protects persisted runtime storage. title: Security Boundaries and Remaining Limits
preview: The implemented security layer is meaningful, but it must be described honestly. The project demonstrates baseline infrastructure hardening suitable for an academic distributed platform; it does not claim to be a finished enterprise security program. preview2: d Trino access; SSH-based remote Spark submission; encrypted runtime storage support on the Linux nodes. title: Conclusion
preview: This chapter showed that security is integrated into as an architectural layer rather than a superficial add-on. Identity is controlled through Kerberos, browser-based Hadoop access is protected through SPNEGO and HTTPS, analytical exposure is filtered through an authenticated Trino gateway, remote Spark submission is secured operationally through SSH, and encrypted runtime storage strengthens protection at rest. The
preview2: chapter also made clear that the implemented security posture is honest in scope: it is strong enough to be technically meaningful and academically defensible, while still distinct from a full enterprise security stack. The next chapter focuses on how this distributed and secured platform was validated through readiness checks, pipeline execution, observability, and demonstration evidence.
